summary: Pulseframe is an offline-first health station for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth is delayed or unavailable. It brings daily health tracking into one app: a checklist, vital signs, exercise, radiation dose and mood check-ins. It learns each crew member's personal baseline and flags unusual readings with plain-language explanations. A guided emergency mode, a 3D body map and a voice-enabled assistant limited to the onboard kit support the crew in a crisis. Built on NASA research, it supports decisions; it never replaces a flight surgeon.
details:
What it does: Pulseframe is an offline-first health station for astronauts on long missions, where help from Earth is delayed or unavailable. It covers NASA's five spaceflight hazards in one app:

  • Dashboard: seven-day vital-sign trends.
  • Personal-baseline alerts: each astronaut's own normal is learned, and unusual readings are flagged with plain-language reasons.
  • Daily checklist: medications, vitals, exercise, radiation and mood.
  • Logs: fitness, radiation dose and psych check-ins.
  • Emergency mode: guides the crew in eight steps, using a 3D body map and onboard protocol cards.
  • AI assistant: limited to the onboard medical kit, with a floating voice mic.

Impact: Pulseframe gives crews medical independence, catches problems early, saves crew time and reduces stress in emergencies. The same approach could help remote places on Earth.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, IndexedDB (offline storage), Recharts, Three.js, Zod, the Web Speech API, optional Groq AI, Vitest (125 tests), Figma, Blender, GitHub and Vercel.

Creativity: Alerts compare each astronaut with their own baseline, every alert and suggestion explains itself, the AI can only recommend items that are on board, the 3D body is used to pinpoint the problem, and voice input works hands-free.

Factors considered: The app works fully offline because of communication delays. For safety it is decision support only: it never suggests doses and a flight surgeon must approve treatment. Its guidance comes from more than 130 public sources, mainly NASA. Health data stays on the device and the demo uses simulated data only. It is quick to use, with big buttons, voice input and mobile layouts.
